title: Sour Suppresses Sweet, Salty, and Bitter: Implications for Signal Processing in Taste Buds
abstract:
Taste is typically encountered as complex blends, yet how peripheral taste organs process heterogeneous mixtures remains poorly understood. Here we asked how sour stimuli influence the encoding of sweet, salty, and bitter tastes in primary gustatory sensory neurons. Using in vivo calcium imaging in mice of either sex to record neurons in geniculate ganglia during oral delivery of tastants, we compared responses to naturally occurring taste stimuli presented alone versus in binary mixtures that activate acid (sour)-sensing (Type III) taste bud cells. Adding citric acid or HCl robustly suppressed sucrose-evoked responses in geniculate ganglion neurons, even though acid itself did not activate those neurons. Acid-induced suppression generalized to bitter and salty tastes, which, like sucrose, are believed to activate Type II taste cells. Additional stimuli that activate acid-sensing taste cells (NH
                     4 
                    Cl, KCl) also reduced sucrose responses, supporting a common mechanism linked to Type III cells. Manipulating levels of serotonin (a paracrine transmitter released by Type III cells) in taste buds altered taste suppression: increasing serotonin with 5-hydroxytryptophan enhanced acid-induced suppression whereas depleting serotonin with para-chlorophenylalanine weakened it. Finally, population analyses, including UMAP dimensionality reduction, indicate that taste suppression is not limited to a particular subset of gustatory sensory neurons. The findings are consistent with serotonin-dependent paracrine inhibition within taste buds as a contributor to sour-driven suppression in taste mixtures and reveal a compression of gustatory information into hedonic categories as early as at the level of primary sensory neurons.
                   
                   
                     Significance Statement 
                    Foods typically present a complex mixture of tastes. However, understanding how the nervous system processes gustatory signals has traditionally relied on investigations that analyze responses to individual tastes. Our study investigates how mixtures of naturally occurring food tastes activate sensory neurons and how emergent signals arise when combinations of gustatory stimuli excite taste buds. Using in vivo imaging of primary gustatory neurons in mice, we show that sour stimuli suppress neural responses to sweet, bitter, and salty tastes. The findings reveal an early, peripheral stage of neural computation that helps explain how complex flavors are encoded.

title: Rotigotine Behenate ameliorates depression in Parkinson's disease through NF-κB-mediated anti-inflammation and BDNF-mediated neuroprotection
abstract: Depression in Parkinson's disease (DPD) is a prevalent non-motor complication that currently lacks effective targeted therapy. We established a combined MPTP/CUMS model in male C57BL/6 mice, which induced a higher incidence of depression and more stable depressive-like phenotypes than MPTP-only modeling and closely recapitulated clinical DPD pathology. Pearson correlation analysis confirmed severe dopamine (DA) and 5-hydroxytryptamine (5-HT) dysregulation predominantly in the striatum (STR) and prefrontal cortex (PFC), identifying these regions as core DPD lesion sites. Behavioral assays demonstrated that ROTB ameliorated both motor dysfunction and depressive-like behavior and restored regional neurotransmitter balance, whereas fluoxetine-included solely as an efficacy comparator for the depressive-like phenotype-did not improve motor symptoms. Mechanistically, ROTB suppressed NF-κB/NLRP3-mediated neuroinflammation and activated the BDNF/TrkB/PI3K/Akt/GSK-3β cascade, elevating synaptic protein levels and reversing dendritic spine loss. Pharmacological inhibition of the NF-κB pathway with QNZ only partially recapitulated the antidepressant effects of ROTB, indicating the existence of NF-κB-independent protective mechanisms. In summary, ROTB alleviates DPD through NF-κB-mediated anti-inflammation and BDNF-mediated neuroprotection, offering preclinical evidence for DPD therapy.

title: Electromyography of the Tongue in Mechanically Ventilated Patients with Acute Brain Injury and Healthy Volunteers
abstract: Assessment of upper airway function in ventilated patients with acute brain injury is important for extubation but limited by impaired consciousness and the endotracheal tube. As a marker of upper airway function, we investigated tongue electromyography (EMG) in healthy controls and mechanically ventilated patients with acute brain injury. In healthy participants, non-invasive tongue EMG was recorded during rest, deep breathing (nasal and oral), partially obstructed nasal breathing, and voluntary motor activation through pressing the tongue laterally against the molar teeth. In patients, EMG was recorded at baseline and during individualised physiological challenges involving modifications to ventilatory or oxygen support to increase upper airway stress. Follow-up recordings were obtained in six patients 2-4 days after baseline. External hypoglossal nerve stimulation yielded Compound Muscle Action Potentials (CMAPs). We define Glossal Function Index (GFI; EMG - CMAP Area-Under-Curve (AUC) ratio) and Rhythmic Involuntary Frequency (RIF) i.e., rate of prominent EMG peaks. We recruited 10 healthy participants and 10 patients. Taking the mean over 5 readings per participant, CMAP-AUC had median value 25 mVms (IQR 19-31 mVms) for healthy participants, and 12 mVms (IQR 9-15 mVms) amongst patients. Voluntary motor activation of the tongue yielded the highest median healthy-participant GFI (79 (IQR 53-90); other manoeuvres: 8 (IQR 5-19)). RIF demonstrated consistent rhythmic activity in healthy participants (median 13.4 peaks/min (IQR 11.2-14.9 peaks/min); 2/60 readings aperiodic). Patients frequently demonstrated irregular or arhythmic activity (median 8.5 peaks/min (IQR 8.1-10.1 peaks/min); 8/25 readings aperiodic). RIF matches EMG morphology of patients with frequent isolated bursts and greater periodicity during ventilator challenge and follow-up. Non-invasive tongue EMG characterised upper airway muscle activity in healthy individuals and ventilated patients with acute brain injury; GFI and RIF are novel markers for further evaluation in predicting extubation success.

title: System-level nonequivalence between integrated information and expected free energy in noisy permutation networks
abstract: The free-energy principle (FEP) and active inference describe prediction and adaptation using generative models, whereas integrated information theory (IIT) examines intrinsic causal organization. Can knowledge of a network's prediction in its current state determine its intrinsic integration? We address this question using a fixed one-step state-risk expected free energy (EFE) and IIT system integrated information. Noisy binary permutation networks allow causal wiring to vary while local transition reliability remains fixed. From a homogeneous current state, different architectures have identical complete one-step predictive distributions, and thus identical EFE under common preferences and observation models. Nevertheless, multicycle architectures have zero whole-system IIT integration, while single cycles can be integrated. For an n-unit noisy single cycle with reliability η, we obtain the exact expression φsnη=min{2ηnlog22η,-nlog2η}. We prove that the minimum-information partition cuts exactly two causal edges, establish a unique interior maximum, and show that, in the large-n limit, the optimal reliability approaches unity, the joint specified-state probability approaches one half, and the maximum system integrated information approaches one ibit. Independent computation corroborates these results. Local surprisal-coordinate identities can be expressed through optimized variational free energy under exact inference, but this algebraic identity does not establish that a neural system performs variational inference. The counterexample establishes a state-conditioned non-identifiability limit for the specified EFE, not an incompatibility between IIT and the FEP. Bridging the two descriptions requires intervention-sensitive information beyond this single predictive distribution.

title: Digital Parenting and Parent-Reported Internet Gaming Disorder-Related Symptoms Among Children: A Cross-Sectional Study
abstract: Background/Objectives: Internet Gaming Disorder (IGD)-related symptoms are a concern for children’s digital mental health, yet evidence on digital parenting as a family-context correlate of these symptoms is limited. This study examined the concurrent associations of total digital parenting and its two operational dimensions, Digital Knowledge and Technical Competence (DKTC) and Digital Guidance, Protection, and Engagement (DGPE), with parent-reported IGD-related symptom severity. Methods: This cross-sectional survey included 285 parent reports from Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, each concerning one child aged 6–13 years (M = 8.76, SD = 1.32; 55.4% boys). Parents completed an adapted parent-report IGDS9-SF and a 15-item digital-parenting scale. Correlations and hierarchical regression with HC3 standard errors and bootstrap intervals were used. Results: Symptom severity was inversely associated with total digital parenting (r = −0.747), DKTC (r = −0.658), and DGPE (r = −0.710), all p < 0.001. The model containing the two dimensions accounted for 56.0% of the variance, nearly identical to the model containing the total score (55.9%); both dimensions showed unique inverse associations (β = −0.333 and −0.481, p < 0.001). Conclusions: Higher digital parenting was associated with lower parent-reported IGD-related symptom severity. Because the data were cross-sectional and reported by the same parent, causal or protective effects cannot be inferred.

title: Factor Structure, Measurement Invariance, and IRT Analysis of the Internet Gaming Disorder Scale—Short-Form (IGDS9-SF) in Mexican Adolescents
abstract: The Internet Gaming Disorder Scale-Short Form (IGDS9-SF) is widely used to assess Internet Gaming Disorder (IGD) based on the DSM-5 criteria; however, evidence of its psychometric properties in Latin America populations remains limited. This study examined the reliability and validity of the IGDS9-SF in a sample of 782 school-attending Mexican adolescents aged 12–18 years. Psychometric evidence was evaluated through analyses of internal structure, internal consistency, measurement invariance across sex and educational level, item functioning using Item Response Theory (IRT), and nomological validity. The IGDS9-SF showed evidence of a unidimensional structure, with excellent model fit and good internal consistency (ω = 0.85–0.87) Measurement invariance analyses supported scalar invariance across sex and educational level, although strict invariance was not established. Differential item functioning analyses identified statistically significant differences for the items assessing tolerance, escape, and jeopardizing relationships items; however, all effects sizes were trivial (∆R2 McFadden < 0.02) indicating negligible practical impact. IRT analyses showed that most items exhibited strong discrimination, particularly those assessing preoccupation, withdrawal, and tolerance, whereas the deception and escape items showed comparatively weaker performance. The test information curve indicated that the IGDS9-SF provided the greatest measurement precision at moderate to high levels of the latent trait. Nomological validity was supported by significant correlations with measures of internet addiction, depressive symptoms, anxiety, negative gaming consequences and online social capital. Overall, these findings provide psychometric support for using the IGDS9-SF to assess IGD symptoms in school-attending Mexican adolescents.

title: Gaming Addiction and Cognitive Function in Adolescents and Young Adults: A Two-Phase Cross-Sectional Study
abstract:
Background: 
                     Gaming addiction is increasingly prevalent among adolescents and young adults, yet its relationship with cognitive function remains ambiguous. Contradictory findings from past research indicate a need for further investigation. 
                   
                   
                     Aim: 
                     To assess the relationship between gaming addiction and cognitive functions in adolescents and young adults. 
                   
                   
                     Methods: 
                     A two-phase cross-sectional study was conducted among 315 participants aged 18–25. In Phase I, the Gaming Addiction Scale (GAS) and lifestyle habits were assessed in the full sample. In Phase II, 50 gaming addicts (GAS ≥ 4) and 50 non-addicts (GAS ≤ 2) were randomly selected for cognitive testing using Addenbrooke’s Cognitive Examination (ACE-III), the Stroop Word Color Test, and P300 event-related potential. 
                   
                   
                     Results: 
                     
                      The gaming addiction prevalence was 13.5%. Addicts had significantly lower total ACE-III scores (87.8 ± 3.98) than non-addicts (91.14 ± 2.87), particularly in attention, memory, and language domains (
                       P < 0 
                      .001), and took longer on Stroop color- and word-naming tasks (
                       P =  
                      0.02, 0.005). P300 latency and amplitude did not differ significantly between groups. GAS scores correlated negatively with ACE-III domains and positively with Stroop durations.
                     
                   
                   
                     Conclusion: 
                     Gaming addiction was associated with lower attention, memory, and language scores on univariate analysis; after adjusting for age, gender, fitness, and screen time, only the memory association remained robust, language was borderline, and attention was no longer independent. Behavioral differences were significant, but P300 differences were not significant; given the cross-sectional design, this does not indicate that cognitive deficits precede brain changes. Longitudinal studies are needed to clarify this relationship.

title: Hydrogen-rich saline alleviates inflammation-associated depression-like behaviors in mice
abstract: Despite the crucial role of inflammation in depression-like behavior, the low blood-brain barrier penetration of existing anti-inflammatory agents presents a substantial obstacle to effective treatment. Owing to the excellent blood-brain barrier permeability and anti-inflammatory ability of hydrogen-rich saline, this study explores its therapeutic effects on lipopolysaccharide-induced inflammation-associated depression-like behavior in mice. In this study, mice intraperitoneally received lipopolysaccharide (0.83 mg/kg). Thirty minutes later, they intraperitoneally received hydrogen-rich saline (5 mL/kg). Results showed that hydrogen-rich saline significantly alleviated anxiety- and depression-like behaviors in lipopolysaccharide-treated mice, as assessed by open field tests, elevated plus maze tests, forced swim tests, and the tail suspension test. Peripheral inflammation was significantly reduced, associated with inhibited splenomegaly and decreased serum levels of interleukin-1β and tumor necrosis factor-α. Central inflammation was also decreased, related to the reduced number of activated microglia, inhibition of Tolllike receptor 4/myeloid differentiation primary response 88/nuclear factor-κB signaling, and repaired synaptic damage in the hippocampus. These findings suggest that early hydrogen-rich saline administration may attenuate lipopolysaccharide-induced inflammation-associated depression-like behaviors, at least in part, by suppressing microglial pro-inflammatory activation and Tolllike receptor 4/nuclear factor-κB signaling.

title: Adaptation of DECIDE, a Shared Decision Making Intervention, to Improve Perinatal Mental Health Care in Health Systems
abstract: Effectively engaging and communicating with perinatal individuals is crucial in meeting the unique decision needs of perinatal individuals, particularly those with anxiety, depression, or other mental health disorders. This study adapted DECIDE, a shared decision making intervention proven to be effective in behavioral health care for adults with psychiatric disorders. The adaptation was to improve perinatal care providers' competency in patient engagement and communication in health systems' perinatal care delivery. In this paper, we report on the adaptation strategies and processes for embedding DECIDE provider training into perinatal health and mental health care delivery. The Iterative Decision-making for Evaluation of Adaptation (IDEA) and the Framework for Reporting Adaptations and Modifications-Enhanced (FRAME) guided the adaptation of the DECIDE provider training. The adaptation of the DECIDE provider training was conducted in four phases: (1) conducting a literature review of empirical evidence, (2) engaging perinatal health and mental health care providers and content experts, (3) identifying and making specific content adaptations and developing clinical vignettes to fit perinatal care settings, and (4) recording the adapted training and new video illustrations and launching the adapted DECIDE for MOM provider training. The adaptation process engaged perinatal mental health and healthcare providers and experts in health systems as well as those who were part of the original DECIDE development and implementation team. After the two rounds of feedback, revision and consensus process, we finalized the training content, created clinical vignettes and filmed case illustrations based on the vignettes. After the iterative editing process of recorded modules and case illustration videos, the finalized DECIDE for MOM provider training was launched on Canvas in August 2025. The next step is to conduct feasibility evaluation of the adapted training by implementing the DECIDE for MOM provider training in health systems.

title: Concordance and validity of federated versus centralized analyses in treatment-resistant depression
abstract: To evaluate whether federated analyses can reproduce centralized results for treatment-resistant depression (TRD) risk prediction using privacy-preserving statistical models. We conducted a retrospective cohort study of 7272 adults with incident major depressive disorder initiating antidepressants (2015-2021) in Maccabi Healthcare Services, Israel. Treatment-resistant depression was defined as progression to third-line regimens within 24 months. Data were geographically partitioned into 2 nodes to simulate federation. Federated generalized linear and Cox models were estimated using privacy-preserving iteratively reweighted least squares with cross-validated feature selection. Agreement with centralized analyses was assessed using coefficient differences, statistical-significance concordance, and confidence interval (CI) overlap. Model performance was evaluated using discrimination, calibration, and fairness metrics. Federated and centralized models showed near-perfect concordance. Feature selection produced almost identical predictor sets, and coefficient estimates were strongly aligned, with mean absolute differences <0.01, complete decision agreement among predictors retained by both models, and >95% CI overlap. Predictive performance was modest but consistent across settings (AUC ∼0.65 for logistic; ∼0.62 for Cox), with preserved calibration and similar subgroup patterns. Federated models reproduced major clinical associations observed centrally, including higher TRD risk with prior antidepressant exposure, psychiatric hospitalization, anxiety and personality disorders, and polypharmacy, and lower risk with atrial fibrillation and delayed therapy initiation. Results show that federated implementations of standard epidemiologic models can retain the validity and stability of centralized analyses, even for complex psychiatric outcomes requiring high-dimensional adjustment. Federated analysis can closely replicate centralized statistical model results while preserving privacy, supporting its use for scalable, multi-institutional epidemiologic research.

title: Dynamic associations between received social support, PTSD, and depressive symptoms during post-burn recovery
abstract: Background: Social support is an important determinant of psychological adjustment following trauma, yet its temporal relationship with posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and depressive symptoms remains incompletely understood among burn survivors. The present study examined the dynamic associations between received social support, PTSD symptoms, and depressive symptoms during the first two years following burn injury.Method: A total of 118 adult burn patients were recruited from the largest burn centre in Taiwan. Received social support, PTSD symptoms, and depressive symptoms were assessed at 3, 6, 12, and 24 months post-burn. Four-wave cross-lagged panel analyses were conducted to examine longitudinal associations among these variables.Results: Higher levels of received social support at 3 months predicted lower PTSD symptoms and depressive symptoms at 6 months. In contrast, higher depressive symptoms at 12 months predicted lower received social support at 24 months. No significant associations were observed between PTSD symptoms and subsequent social support.Conclusions: Early received social support may promote psychological adjustment following burn injury, whereas persistent depressive symptoms may contribute to later reductions in social support.

title: The Natural History of Spinocerebellar Ataxia Types 7 and 8
abstract: Spinocerebellar ataxias are genetically heterogeneous neurodegenerative disorders characterized by progressive cerebellar degeneration. Among them, SCA7 and SCA8 are particularly rare, and their longitudinal natural history has not been well defined. Using data from the Clinical Research Consortium for the Study of Cerebellar Ataxias, we examined disease progression in genetically confirmed SCA7 and SCA8 patients in North America. Longitudinal changes in motor severity were assessed using the Scale for the Assessment and Rating of Ataxia (SARA), alongside cognitive function (Cerebellar Cognitive Affective Syndrome scale [CCAS]) and depressive symptoms (Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9)), applying linear mixed-effects models with genetic and clinical covariates. Our cohort included 27 individuals with SCA7 and 51 with SCA8 with baseline data, among which 22 individuals with SCA7 and 42 with SCA8 have longitudinal follow-up. Age at onset in SCA7 was inversely associated with pathologic repeat length (β = -1.43, p < 0.01), whereas no significant correlation was observed in SCA8 (β = -0.08, p = 0.28). Longitudinal analyses demonstrated that SCA7 progressed relatively rapidly, with SARA scores worsening by 1.68 points per year, while SCA8 showed substantially slower progression at 0.47 points per year. In both disorders, progression was predominantly driven by deterioration in the axial SARA domain, particularly gait and stance. In contrast, CCAS and PHQ-9 scores remained stable over approximately 5 years of follow-up, with no significant longitudinal changes detected. These findings demonstrate distinct disease trajectories between SCA7 and SCA8 to inform future longitudinal studies and therapeutic trials.

title: Urban heat radiation and health perception in Addis Ababa
abstract: Exposure to high temperatures poses a multidimensional health hazard. Low- and middle-income countries are likely to experience large increases in average annual temperature due to climate change. Ethiopia is expected to warm by up to 4 °C by 2100. We investigated the association between land surface temperature (LST) and health-related quality of life (HRQOL). This is, to our knowledge, one of the first studies of its kind to be conducted in a large African urban cohort. We analyzed cross-sectional data from the COMBAT cohort in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, collected in January 2025 (N = 3201). HRQOL was assessed using the EQ-5D-5L; the outcome variables were the utility index and its five dimensions. LST exposure was characterized using baseline and proximal metrics. We used a beta-one-inflated regression and logistic regression to assess associations. Overall, 53.6% of participants reported problems in at least one EQ-5D-5L dimension, with anxiety or depression being the most frequent (33.5%). Individuals reporting problems were exposed to a slightly higher median baseline LST (32.73 vs. 32.43 °C). We observed a consistent inverted U-shaped association between LST and the probability of reporting perfect health. The probability of reporting problems increased at higher LST values in usual activities, self-care, and anxiety or depression. The results suggest that deviations from the local thermal average are negatively associated with perceived health. This study illustrates the potential value of integrating HRQOL indicators into public health surveillance to enable timely intervention against the health impacts of climate change.

title: Identifying characteristics and behavioral phenotypes of musculoskeletal disorders using wearables in All of Us
abstract: Wearable devices provide continuous measures of daily activity, sleep, and heart-rate (HR)-derived characteristics, creating new opportunities for digital phenotyping of musculoskeletal disorders (MSD). However, longitudinal behavioral patterns and heterogeneity among individuals with MSD remain poorly understood. This study aimed to identify characteristics associated with MSD and characterize behavioral phenotypes using longitudinal wearable data. We analyzed 2344 participants (MSD = 1036; non-MSD = 1308) from the All of Us Research Program. First, supervised machine-learning models were trained using sociodemographic, physical measurement, and wearable-derived features to distinguish individuals with and without MSD and identify factors associated with MSD status. Model interpretation was performed using SHapley Additive exPlanations values. Second, temporal profiling and unsupervised clustering were applied to 90-day wearable trajectories of participants with MSD to identify behavioral phenotypes. XGBoost achieved the best classification performance (accuracy = 0.929, area under the receiver operating characteristic curve = 0.930, area under the precision-recall curve = 0.870, F1 = 0.919). Important factors associated with MSD included lower activity, longer sleep, and female sex. Behavioral phenotyping identified 5 distinct phenotypes differing in activity patterns, sleep characteristics, HR-derived measures, pain burden, mental health conditions, and employment status. Notably, high-pain phenotypes exhibited greater prevalence of anxiety and depressive disorders, lower pulse rate variability, and distinct sleep profiles compared with more active phenotypes. These phenotypes demonstrated moderate reproducibility in bootstrap-based stability analysis (mean adjusted rand index = 0.62). Longitudinal wearable data revealed behavioral heterogeneity among individuals with MSD that was not fully explained by traditional diagnostic categories. These findings demonstrate the value of wearable-based digital phenotyping for characterizing differences in daily functioning and symptom burden among individuals with MSD. Wearable-derived behavioral phenotyping provides a complementary approach for understanding heterogeneity in MSD and may support future efforts in patient monitoring, stratification, and personalized management.

title: A Transcriptomic Analysis of Putative Gustatory Receptor Genes in Two Hawkmoth Species ( Lapara coniferarum and Sphinx dollii )
journal: Archives of Insect Biochemistry and Physiology
abstract:
ABSTRACT 
                   
                    Chemoreception in insects relies heavily on multiple ancient groups of receptors, including those used for sensing sweet and bitter tastes. Gustatory receptors (GRs) allow individuals to locate hostplants via short‐range chemical sensing and can be especially useful in finding foodplants for nectaring and oviposition. When comparing diverse insect groups, such as hawkmoths, GR gene sequences can show a great deal of gains and losses across taxa. Previously, GRs have been identified in many model insect groups, however, non‐model insects lack sequence data and GR expression data remains under‐studied. However, putative GRs can be identified using
                     de novo 
                    transcriptomes. Here, we examined two different hawkmoths (Lepidoptera: Sphingidae: Sphinginae: Sphigina) for gustatory receptor expression differences based on variation in adult feeding behavior. Adult
                     Lapara coniferarum 
                    (non‐feeding) exhibited fewer sugar‐taste gustatory receptor genes than adult
                     Sphinx dollii 
                    (feeding) individuals. These results reveal that gustatory receptor genes can be identified using published genomes and newly generated transcriptomes while providing a model for identifying gustatory receptor expression in non‐model insects.

title: Individual differences in blood-brain barrier permeability are associated with childhood trauma and circulating immune markers in major depressive disorder: Preliminary findings
abstract: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is a major public health challenge, and childhood trauma is an important risk factor for its development. The blood-brain barrier (BBB) regulates communication between the peripheral immune system and the brain, but how childhood trauma and circulating immune alterations relate to BBB permeability in MDD remains unclear. We studied 39 participants with MDD and 22 healthy controls (HC). Childhood trauma was assessed using the Childhood Trauma Questionnaire (CTQ), BBB permeability was measured using dynamic contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging, and circulating leukocyte subtypes and immune-related proteins were quantified in blood. Covariate-adjusted linear models accounted for age, gender, body mass index, race, ethnicity, and current psychiatric medication where applicable. Blood-brain barrier (BBB) permeability did not differ significantly between participants with MDD and HC. Within the MDD group, higher whole-brain BBB permeability was associated with greater childhood trauma, specifically higher CTQ total, emotional abuse, and physical abuse scores, as well as higher circulating monocyte and neutrophil counts. In a hypothesis-driven analysis based on our prior work, higher plasma matrix metalloproteinase 8 (MMP8) was associated with higher BBB permeability. In an exploratory Olink screen, fibroblast growth factor 21 (FGF21) was the only protein associated with whole-brain BBB permeability after correction for multiple testing, with higher FGF21 related to lower permeability. The corresponding whole-brain associations were not significant in HC. Our preliminary findings identify dimensional associations of BBB permeability with childhood trauma and circulating immune measures within MDD, without evidence of a disorder-level increase in BBB permeability. They support further investigation of the BBB as a potential interface linking childhood adversity and peripheral immune processes in depression, while requiring replication in larger longitudinal samples.

title: Modulation of neuroimmunity by early-life microbiota colonization
abstract: Early life (fetal period to 2-3 y postnatally) is a critical window for the coordinated development of the intestine, lungs, and brain. As core pathways mediating microbe-immune-neuron crosstalk, the gut-brain and lung-brain axes drive cross-organ communication via early-life microbiota colonization, profoundly shaping immune maturation and neurodevelopmental trajectories. During fetal development, maternal microbial metabolites cross the placenta to prime in utero immune and neural development. After birth, rapid microbial colonization occurs in the intestine and lungs. Through signaling molecules including short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), tryptophan metabolites, and bacterial extracellular vesicles (BEVs), coupled with vagal nerve and mucosal immune pathways, the microbiota maintains intestinal and pulmonary immune homeostasis, preserves blood-brain barrier (BBB) integrity, and modulates microglial activation, thereby regulating neurogenesis, synaptic pruning, and brain functional programming. Early-life dysbiosis is commonly associated with preterm birth, cesarean delivery, infection, and antibiotic exposure. In human observational studies, it accompanies disrupted organ homeostasis and neuroinflammatory signatures, and is linked to an increased long-term risk of autism spectrum disorder (ASD), attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), and intellectual disability; in neonatal animal models, it aggravates hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy (HIE) and encephalopathy of prematurity. Because dysbiosis frequently co-occurs with prematurity, infection, and other confounders, these associations do not by themselves establish causality. This review summarizes early-life colonization patterns of intestinal and pulmonary microbiota and their underlying neuroimmune mechanisms, analyzes the impacts of dysbiosis on neuroimmunity and related diseases, and proposes intervention strategies, aiming to provide a theoretical basis for neonatal health protection and neurodevelopmental disorder prevention.

title: An Anti-Adhesive Hydrogel Delivering Ginger-Derived Exosome-Like Nanoparticles Reshapes the Neuroinflammatory Microenvironment After Traumatic Brain Injury
abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) triggers secondary injury involving neuroinflammation, oxidative stress, and mitochondrial dysfunction, highlighting the need for multi-target therapies. Ginger-derived exosome-like nanoparticles (GELNs) offer multi-target therapeutic potential but are limited by insufficient local retention and rapid clearance. TBI-induced brain-skull adhesion may further aggravate the pathological environment. To address these limitations, an anti-adhesive hydrogel (CG) composed of methacrylated chondroitin sulfate and 2-methacryloyloxyethyl phosphorylcholine is loaded with GELNs to form CG-GELNs. CG-GELNs attenuates pathological brain-skull adhesion and provides greater behavioral benefits than free GELNs, including reduced anxiety-like behavior, improved social novelty discrimination, and enhanced spatial memory. At the pathological level, CG-GELNs confers coordinated protection against secondary injury by preserving blood-brain barrier integrity, suppressing pro-inflammatory responses, mitigating mitochondrial damage and oxidative stress, and ultimately preserving synaptic function. Mechanistically, GELNs-associated microRNA-396 (miR-396) suppresses secreted phosphoprotein 1 (SPP1) expression, and functional rescue experiments support the contribution of this miR-396/SPP1 axis to the anti-inflammatory effects of GELNs in microglial cells. Overall, CG-GELNs simultaneously improves localized delivery of GELNs, attenuates pathological brain-skull adhesion, and suppresses neuroinflammation, offering a potentially translatable therapeutic platform for remodeling the neuroinflammatory microenvironment and promoting neurological recovery after TBI.

title: Serum Extracellular Vesicle Proteomics Identifies Candidate Protein Biomarkers for Major Depressive Disorder with a Diagnostic Specificity Assessment against Schizophrenia
abstract: Diagnosis of major depressive disorder (MDD) relies on subjective criteria and lacks objective biomarkers. Serum extracellular vesicles (EVs) carry stable cargo and can cross the blood-brain barrier, making them attractive biomarker sources. We therefore profiled serum EVs from a discovery cohort of 60 participants (40 healthy controls [HCs], 20 MDD patients) by size-exclusion chromatography and liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry, and subsequently validated candidate proteins by ELISA in an independent cohort of 60 participants (20 HCs, 20 MDD, 20 patients with schizophrenia [SCZ]). Differentially expressed proteins (DEPs) were defined by |log2 fold change| > 1 and Benjamini-Hochberg FDR-adjusted q < 0.05. Using these criteria, we identified 358 DEPs (235 upregulated, 123 downregulated), which were enriched in complement activation, coagulation, and immune-inflammatory pathways. However, several of the most significant DEPs are abundant circulating plasma proteins that are common co-isolates of serum EVs, so part of this signal may reflect residual soluble serum protein, and-given that EVs were isolated from serum rather than platelet-poor plasma-the pathway enrichment should be interpreted with caution. In the validation cohort, EV-associated TNC and APLP1 were elevated and EV-associated TF was reduced in MDD relative to HCs (P < 0.05), whereas only serum APLP1 was elevated. Notably, EV-associated TNC was also elevated in SCZ, while APLP1 and TF were unchanged; moreover, direct MDD-versus-SCZ comparisons were not significant, indicating that the data do not support MDD-specific alterations. In addition, a logistic-regression model combining EV-associated APLP1, TF and TNC distinguished MDD from HCs with an area under the curve of 0.905 (95% CI 0.812-0.998; 0.830 by leave-one-out cross-validation), outperforming individual proteins (TF 0.725; TNC 0.758; APLP1 0.725). Collectively, these findings define a serum EV-associated proteomic signature in MDD and preliminarily validate TF, TNC and APLP1 as candidate diagnostic biomarkers, implicating immune-inflammatory and complement-related pathways. Nevertheless, the panel remains exploratory and requires validation in larger, multi-center cohorts with diverse psychiatric controls.

title: Modernizing reporting and communication of isolated echogenic intracardiac foci and choroid plexus cysts in the cell-free DNA era
abstract: Echogenic intracardiac foci and choroid plexus cysts are among the most common findings on second-trimester prenatal ultrasound. Historically classified as "soft markers," they were incorporated into aneuploidy risk assessment in an era when screening relied on maternal age and serum analytes with limited performance. The widespread adoption of cell-free DNA (cfDNA) screening has fundamentally altered this paradigm. With detection rates exceeding 99% for trisomy 21, the modest likelihood ratios associated with isolated EIF and CPC no longer meaningfully alter post-test probability or clinical management. These findings are therefore best regarded as common normal variants rather than clinically significant markers of aneuploidy. Despite this transformation in prenatal screening, reporting and communication practices have changed little and remain highly variable, often influenced by historical practice patterns and medicolegal concerns rather than contemporary evidence. Numerous studies demonstrate that disclosure of isolated EIF and CPC may result in maternal anxiety, persistent concern despite reassurance, unnecessary diagnostic testing, and disruption of maternal-fetal bonding. These effects may be amplified by immediate patient access to ultrasound reports and terminology that continues to imply pathology where none exists. This review examines the historical and contemporary evidence supporting a modernized approach to the reporting and communication of isolated EIF and CPC in the era of cfDNA screening and proposes an evidence-based framework for clinical practice. In pregnancies with low-risk cfDNA results and a normal detailed fetal anatomic survey, isolated EIF and CPCs should be regarded as benign findings without clinical significance. Contemporary evidence no longer supports the routine reporting and communication of these findings in the context of aneuploidy risk. When disclosure occurs, communication should be non-alarmist, emphasize that these are normal variants, and avoid terminology suggesting increased risk for chromosomal abnormalities. Aligning reporting and communication with current evidence has the potential to reduce patient harm while promoting patient-centered prenatal care.

title: Beyond weakness: The overlooked cognitive face of myasthenia gravis
abstract: Myasthenia gravis (MG) is an autoimmune disease mediated by autoantibodies. Traditionally, it was strictly defined as a neuromuscular junction-specific disorder, believed not to affect the central nervous system (CNS). However, recent clinical observations and neuropsychological studies have demonstrated that a significant proportion of MG patients exhibit cognitive dysfunction, with clinical manifestations encompassing impairments in multiple cognitive domains such as verbal fluency, information processing speed, and memory. Neuroimaging further reveals structural and functional alterations in MG patients, including gray matter volume atrophy and abnormalities in default mode network connectivity. These findings challenge previous cognitive frameworks, suggesting that the disease may exert broader effects on the CNS. Current understanding indicates that the pathogenesis of MG-associated cognitive impairment involves complex central-peripheral interactions: mechanisms such as blood-brain barrier disruption, cross-reaction of specific autoantibodies, and neuroinflammatory responses can lead to direct CNS involvement, whereas chronic hypoxia (secondary to respiratory muscle weakness or sleep apnea), prolonged drug effects, and psychological factors like depression and anxiety associated with the disease may also indirectly impair cognitive function. Nevertheless, the field still faces numerous challenges, including the lack of large-scale longitudinal studies to elucidate the natural course and trajectory of cognitive impairment, as well as the identification of biomarkers. This narrative review collates recent research advances regarding MG-related cognitive impairment and discusses its clinical manifestations, confounding influencing factors, underlying pathophysiological mechanisms, and existing diagnostic difficulties.

title: Changes in neuroinflammatory and blood-brain barrier-related markers during methylphenidate treatment in children with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder: a prospective observational study
abstract: This study aims to investigate within-participant changes in serum IL-6, S100B, and Claudin-5 levels during 3 months of methylphenidate treatment in children with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), and to examine whether biomarker changes were associated with changes in ADHD symptom severity. This single-center, uncontrolled prospective observational study included 42 medication-naïve children aged 6-11 years with ADHD who completed 3 months of methylphenidate treatment. Serum IL-6, S100B, and Claudin-5 levels were measured at baseline and month 3. ADHD symptom severity was assessed using the Conners Parent Rating Scale-Revised: Short Form (CPRS-R:S) and the Conners Teacher Rating Scale-Revised: Short Form (CTRS-R:S). Associations between percentage changes in biomarkers and symptom scores were examined, with correction for multiple testing. Parent- and teacher-rated ADHD symptom severity decreased significantly over 3 months. Serum IL-6 and S100B levels also decreased significantly, whereas the change in Claudin-5 was not significant. A nominal inverse association was observed between percentage changes in IL-6 and teacher-rated symptom severity, but this association did not remain significant after multiple-testing correction. Among children who completed the 3-month treatment period, methylphenidate was associated with reductions in selected peripheral biomarkers associated with inflammatory and glial processes. However, biomarker changes were not significantly associated with symptom changes after correction for multiple testing, and the uncontrolled observational design does not establish a causal effect of methylphenidate on these biomarkers. ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT07041333, registered on 19 June 2025. Prospectively registered. • Neuroinflammatory and blood-brain barrier-related alterations have been implicated in ADHD, but most available evidence is cross-sectional. • Longitudinal data on biomarker changes during methylphenidate treatment in medication-naïve children are limited. • Three months of methylphenidate treatment was accompanied by reductions in peripheral serum IL-6 and S100B, whereas Claudin-5 did not change significantly. • Within-participant biomarker changes were largely unrelated to symptom changes after correction for multiple testing.

title: Subjective Experience of a Severe Mental Disorder: A Qualitative Study of Siblings' Perspectives
abstract:
ABSTRACT 
                   
                     Background 
                     The subjective experience of siblings of individuals with severe mental disorders (SMDs) remains largely unexamined, despite their critical role within the family system and their growing involvement in informal caregiving. 
                   
                   
                     Aim 
                     To explore in depth the subjective experience of SMD, analyzing the emotional impacts, informal caregiving demands, quality of life and family dynamics. 
                   
                   
                     Method 
                     An exploratory qualitative study involving 60 adult siblings of patients with SMD. Data were collected via semi‐structured interviews and analyzed in accordance with the principles of Grounded Theory. 
                   
                   
                     Results 
                     Qualitative analysis identified four core empirical categories: Subjective Appraisal, Coping, Quality of life, and Family Relationships. Participants described persistent negative emotions (fear, anger, sadness, guilt) that compromised their well‐being and relational dynamics. Ongoing involvement in informal caregiving was characterized as “emotionally draining,” restricting personal trajectories and altering family structures. Grounded in these findings, the emerging theoretical model conceptualizes siblings' resistance as an active, dynamic, and processual phenomenon balancing adaptive and defensive mechanisms. 
                   
                   
                     Conclusion 
                     The sibling experience in SMD is characterized by a substantial emotional and relational strain that remains largely unrecognized in mental health services. Emerging theory suggests that sibling resistance is neither a homogeneous nor a generalizable phenomenon, but rather a dynamic, evolving, and idiosyncratic process. Specific, sustained, and family‐centered interventions are required to address siblings' unique needs as essential stakeholders in care.

title: Collapse of local circuit integrated information Φ during NREM sleep
abstract: Clarifying the mechanisms underlying the emergence of consciousness remains a fundamental challenge in modern neuroscience. Integrated Information Theory (IIT) provides a mathematical framework derived from the phenomenological properties of consciousness as its axioms. IIT proposes that consciousness is identical to a system's intrinsic cause-effect information structure, quantified by integrated information Φ. While IIT predicts that the Φ of a neuronal system should decrease during the loss of consciousness, this hypothesis has remained untested at the neural circuit level. The present study provides empirical support for this IIT prediction. It was found that Φ within local circuits decreases during non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep compared to wakefulness (and REM sleep in the frontal cortex), regardless of cortical laminar structure. The reduction in Φ was particularly pronounced during OFF-periods, when neural activity is collectively suppressed. These results align with IIT's framework, suggesting that the loss of consciousness corresponds to a collapse of integrated information within local circuits. The findings provide empirical support for IIT as a mathematical theory aiming to explain conscious experiences.
